To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cognitive impairment in PD is a progressive process that is associated with a high risk for developing PD dementia.

CD in PD are progressive and have a complex pathogenetic nature, and the risk of dementia is higher in older PD patients, in those with more severe disease, late onset of PD, and with more pronounced premorbidity disturbances of regulative function, memory, visual-spatial and nominative speech functions.

the progression of CD in PD is mostly due the increase in intensity of dysregulations, neurodynamic disorders and visual-spatial dysfunction, as well as insufficiency of the nominative speech function, and the high frequency of the transition of moderate cognitive dysfunction to dementia in PD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the clinical features of CD progression in patients with PD.
CD progression in PD and its relationship to the clinical characteristics of the disease.
the clinical characteristics of CD in PD and their predictors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cognitive impairment (CD) in Parkinson’s disease (PD) has a progressive character mostly because of increase of intensity of neurodynamic disorders, dysregulation, disturbances of visual and spatial functions and, in the some cases, insuficiency of nominative function of speech.

the progression of CD in PD is a result of the interaction of multiple factors including the severity of PD, the severity of premorbid disturbances in regulative and visual functions, the age and the time from the onset of the disease.
CD in PD are progressive and are associated with the increase of severity of the disease, old age and the presence of premorbid disturbances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CD in PD have an early onset and a progressive character.
cognitive dysfunction in PD have a dynamic character and are associated with the progression of the disease.

CD in PD are progressive and the risk factors of CD progression are: old age, late-onset, severity of disease, more pronounced premorbi disturbances of regulative, visual-spatial and nominative speech functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD in PD are a progressive phenomenon, which can transform into dementia in 2-5-year follow-up.
CD are a common feature of PD and their progression should be taken into account when planning the management of patients with PD.
CD in PD are progressive and the risk factors of CD progression in this group of patients are identified.
